why: Routine AGM notice from a long-established local sailing club domain (2008) that matches her sailing interest and location, asking only whether she will attend.
A prospective client from an aged domain (2012) who booked through her own booking page and references her talk, with no link, payment or credential request.
An IT heads-up that explicitly asks for nothing to be clicked or approved and contains no link, payment or credential request.
A casual note about moving her sailing gear, with no link, request or ask of any kind.
The podcast host writing from the show's own aged domain (2019) about a show-notes correction, linking only to the show's own page and asking for nothing sensitive.
IT impersonation from a personal number pushing a lookalike domain registered six days ago (vennholt-partner.com) to harvest her firm email and password.

An alumni-office message asking her to sign in with her password through an emailed link under an archive deadline; the domain is aged, but she should reach the directory through the school's known site, not this link.
A routine monthly invoice from a long-established supplier domain (2010) with payment details explicitly unchanged and normal 30-day terms.
A mailbox-quota SMS sending her to a lookalike domain registered three days ago, a classic credential-phishing pattern.
A fake network trust-and-safety notice from a lookalike domain registered 19 days ago, using a 7-day threat to make her sign in on the attacker's site.
An accountant's informational note that nothing is due, with no link, payment or credential request.
A plain subscription receipt from her association's aged domain (2010) that asks for nothing.
A generic 'account services' sender asks her to send back a confirmation code sent to her phone, which is one-time-code theft for account takeover.
A recruiter from an aged domain (2018) asks her only to confirm an interview date and explicitly asks for no referees or other data yet.
A renewal demand from an institute that is not her CFA charter body, with a late fee, a threat to her designation and a payment link, aimed at her public credential.
A trustee from an aged domain (2016) asks only who handles new mandates, with no link, money or credential request.
An unknown 'Dale from Thornbeck' on WhatsApp uses legal urgency to get her to phone an unverified number tonight; she should confirm with the host through his known email first.
A registry impersonation from a domain registered 11 days ago uses her public director ID and a deadline to push her to call a mobile helpline number (callback phishing).
An annual officer-record check from the registry's long-established domain (2009) that has no link and needs no action if the details are correct.
A substantive disagreement from a listener at an aged domain (2017) about her published views, with no link or request.
A thank-you note from a listener on an old domain (2009) that asks for nothing.

A bank-details change notice with a new IBAN and a payment instruction is the classic invoice-redirection pattern; even from an aged domain, she should confirm by phone through a known number before paying.
A routine statutory PSC reminder from the registry's long-established domain (2009) with a sensible deadline and a link on that same domain.
A search consultant from an aged domain (2011) following up a call by offering two meeting dates, with no link, money or credential request.
A fake e-signature request trading on her Harborlight talk, from a domain registered five days ago, with a 48-hour expiry and a demand to verify with her email account (credential harvest).
A maintenance notice for her personal site from an aged hosting domain (2011) that says no action is required.
A standard booking-cancellation notification from an aged scheduling domain that points back to her own booking page and asks for nothing.
A standard new-booking notification made through her own booking page, with aged domains throughout and no request beyond attending the call.
